The weakest aspect of the course was the overwhelming number of graded in-class activities introduced after the add-drop period. These activities occurred almost weekly and gradually eroded final grades in a way that felt excessive and discouraging. Rather than supporting learning, they often felt like punitive measures.

Another concern was the instructor’s reluctance to acknowledge and correct mistakes during lectures. This undermined the reliability of the material and gave the impression that ego was prioritized over clarity. In a course where accuracy matters, this was particularly disappointing.

Additionally, the syllabus—which should function as a clear agreement between students and instructor—lacked transparency and consistency. Vague descriptions and unexpected grading elements created confusion and a sense of unfairness.

Overall, this course fell short of Bilkent’s usual academic standards. It was the most regrettable academic experience of my undergraduate studies, not because of the difficulty, but due to its execution and pedagogical approach.
